newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate votes higher Medicare payment for affluent.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate votes higher Medicare payment for affluent.

text.p: Affluent senior citizens could face sharply higher Medicare deductibles for physician's care under a measure approved early Wednesday by a Senate committee.

The Senate Finance Committee also voted to trim to 100,000 a pilot program that originally would have allowed up to 500,000 older Americans to open tax-free medical savings accounts rather than using the traditional Medicare program.
The actions came as the panel debated mammoth legislation needed to implement a five-year balanced budget deal between the White House and Congress.
The measure would cut $115 billion from Medicare and $13.6 billion from the Medicaid program for the poor, elderly and disabled.

By an 18-2 vote the committee approved an amendment by Nebraska Democrat Bob Kerrey forcing affluent seniors to pay higher deductibles under the Medicare Part B program covering doctor's care. The Part B program is voluntary, but nearly all seniors eligible for Medicare choose the coverage.
The current deductible for Medicare Part B is $100 per year and the monthly premium is about $42.50.

Under the plan approved by the committee, senior citizens with incomes $50,000 and above and couples with incomes $75,000 and above would have to meet a higher deductible before the Medicare coverage kicked in.
The higher deductible, based on the premium, would kick in at more than $500 at the $50,000/$75,000 income level and rise to more than $2,000 for the most affluent, aides said.
"It sends a strong message that we are prepared to adjust these mandatory programs, especially the Medicare program, so that it is income-related," Kerrey said.

In another key move, the committee voted 12-8 to cut to 100,000 the medical savings account plan. The accounts are used in conjunction with high deductible insurance policies that kick in for medical emergencies.
Republicans say the medical savings accounts will make seniors more cost-conscious health care shoppers.

The White House says the healthiest seniors will use the tax-free accounts, leaving older, sicker people in Medicare. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the plan would boost Medicare spending by $2 billion.

The overall legislation would save $115 billion in Medicare mainly by cutting payments to doctors, hospitals and other health providers. Seniors would have more choice of managed care plans and would receive an expanded package of preventive benefits.
